    Heatmap Example

    HeatmapExample.Rmd

    For tutorial purposes, SCCNVis comes with example inputs. We will begin by loading them and giving a brief summary of what is in each of them. Note that the length of cell.names is equal to the number of rows in input.matrix and that the length of granges is equal to the number of columns in the input.matrix.

    library(SCCNVis)

set.seed(42)

#Example input matrix
input.matrix <- example.matrix
print(dim(input.matrix))
#> [1] 1000 2813

#Example cell names
cell.names <- example.cells
print(length(cell.names))
#> [1] 1000
print(cell.names[1:3])
#> [1] "cell-1" "cell-2" "cell-3"

#Example GenomicRanges::GRanges obect
granges <- example.granges
print(granges)
#> GRanges object with 2813 ranges and 0 metadata columns:
#>          seqnames            ranges strand
#>             <Rle>         <IRanges>  <Rle>
#>      [1]     chr1   1000000-2000000      *
#>      [2]     chr1   2000000-3000000      *
#>      [3]     chr1   3000000-4000000      *
#>      [4]     chr1   4000000-5000000      *
#>      [5]     chr1   5000000-6000000      *
#>      ...      ...               ...    ...
#>   [2809]     chrY 15000000-16000000      *
#>   [2810]     chrY 16000000-17000000      *
#>   [2811]     chrY 19000000-20000000      *
#>   [2812]     chrY 20000000-21000000      *
#>   [2813]     chrY 21000000-22000000      *
#>   -------
#>   seqinfo: 24 sequences from an unspecified genome; no seqlengths

#Example metadata data.frame object
meta.df <- example.meta
print(head(meta.df))
#>         Sample
#> cell-1 SampleA
#> cell-2 SampleA
#> cell-3 SampleA
#> cell-4 SampleA
#> cell-5 SampleA
#> cell-6 SampleA

#Create a SCCNVis object
obj <- SCCNVis::createPlotObject(input.matrix, cell.names, granges, meta.df)

    The SCCNVis object is a simple object. It contains the input matrix (accessible as obj@Matrix) and the associated GenomicRanges::GRanges object (accessible as obj@GRanges). It also contains metadata associated with each cell, if provided. All plotting functions withing SCCNVis use this object as input.

    For example, a simple heatmap can be created using the following:

    heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj)
print(names(heatmap.result))
#> [1] "Plot"     "PlotData"
print(names(heatmap.result$PlotData))
#> [1] "PlotData"   "Clustering" "Legend"     "Title"

    As you can see, the result is a list object that contains the Plot, which is a ComplexHeatmap object, and the PlotData. In this case, the PlotData is a list containing the actual PlotData (a matrix for the heatmap) and a clustering result, which relates to the row ordering in the heatmap. In this case, it also includes the information for drawing the legend of the plot. These values can be used to create other version of the plot using other packages, or be saved for downstream analysis.

    The resulting file can be saved however you would normally export a ComplexHeatmap. For convenience, it can be saved using the SCCNVis wrapper function for exporting plots. The expected output for the heatmap is also shown below.

    #Example manual method
#png("output/file.png", width=2000, height=500)
#ComplexHeatmap::draw(heatmap.result$Plot,
#     show_heatmap_legend = FALSE,
#     annotation_legend_list = heatmap.result$PlotData$Legend)
#dev.off()

#Simple wrapper for convenience
SCCNVis::saveCustomPlot(heatmap.result, "/path/to/heatmap.png")

    Example 1a. Heatmap

    The heatmap could be further customized if metadata has been provided. At the same time, we may choose to limit our plot to specific regions of interest. For this example, we may choose to focus only on chr7 and chrX, as seen below:

    plot.regions <- example.granges[example.granges@seqnames == "chr7" |
                                  example.granges@seqnames == "chrX",]

#If using a basic annotation as shown here and you want to specify colors,
#it should be provided as a named list
annotation.colors <- list(Sample = c("SampleA" = "red", "SampleB" = "blue"))

heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj,
                                         gr = plot.regions,
                                         annotations = "Sample",
                                         show.annotation.name = TRUE,
                                         annotation.colors = annotation.colors)

    Example 1b. Heatmap of chr7 and chrX, with sample annotation

    We can see that there are at least 2 seemingly distinct clusters present in our heatmap. To simplify our heatmap, we may wish to present the data as a simple average of those groups. To do so, we must add metadata to the SCCNVis object to assign each cell to a group, then tell the makeSCHeatmap function which metadata column to group the cells by. Whenever the heatmap is the result of grouped data, the right side of the plot will show the number of cells described by each group.

    #Calculate distance matrix values
dist <- parallelDist::parallelDist(obj@Matrix)
#Perform hierarchical clustering
hc_re <- hclust(dist, method="ward.D2")
#Split the hierarchical clustering into two groups
kclusters <- cutree(hc_re, k = 2)
obj <- SCCNVis::addMetaData(obj, kclusters, colname = "KClusters")

#If using a grouping method, the way to supply annotation colors changes.
#In this case, they can simply be supplied as a character vector
annotation.colors <- c("blue", "yellow")

heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj,
                                         group = "KClusters",
                                         annotation.colors = annotation.colors)

    Example 1c. Heatmap with pre-specified clusters

    Alternatively, you may create groups using any other method you choose, such as sample of origin, phenotype data, or dynamic clusters. In this example, I use the dynamicTreeCut package to dynamically cluster the cells and group the heatmap using the resulting clusters. I am interested in what proportion of each dynamic cluster comes from each sample, so I set the secondary.group as the Sample metadata column.

    makeSCHeatmap() also accepts custom functions that can be applied to the plot data. The custom function should accept an input data.frame and return a data.frame with the same dimensions and the same row/column order. Column names and row names should not be altered. For visual clarity, let’s add a function that changes all values within 1 standard deviation of the mean to be the mean, so we can focus on whatever strong signals may be present in our data.

    dynamic.kclusters <- dynamicTreeCut::cutreeDynamic(dendro = hc_re, 
                                                   distM = as.matrix(dist),
                                                   deepSplit = 0,
                                                   pamRespectsDendro = TRUE
                                                   )
#>  ..cutHeight not given, setting it to 292  ===>  99% of the (truncated) height range in dendro.
#>  ..done.
names(dynamic.kclusters) <- hc_re$labels
obj <- SCCNVis::addMetaData(obj, dynamic.kclusters, colname = "DynamicKClusters")

custom.func <- function(data) {
  sd.value <- sd(data, na.rm = TRUE)
  mean.value <- mean(data, na.rm = TRUE)
  data[data > mean.value - sd.value & data < mean.value + sd.value] <- mean.value
  return(data)
}


heatmap.result <- SCCNVis::makeSCHeatmap(obj,
                                         group = "DynamicKClusters",
                                         secondary.group = "Sample",
                                         post.plot.mod.fun = custom.func)

    Example 1d. Heatmap with dynamic clusters
